changes_bullets: The integer rule. wz-session-core json gains u64_into and MAX_EXACT_INTEGER (2^53 - 1, the largest integer every JSON reader holds exactly; RFC 7493 draws the same line). Counts, offsets, sizes and millisecond spans stay bare numbers, and so does chain_id, which the writer itself numbers. The payload plane already wrote its values as strings.

Revisions. No key name moves, so no key set, family or carry list moves either; the JSON type of a value does, and this table declares no axis for that, so each row is the whole notice. fields 22 to 23, census 15 to 16, summary 4 to 5, retention 1 to 2, each with the rule in its row and an alias for its key set. The gap sum. A gap is a distance in the session's window, up to 2^62 - 2 at the widest, so seven frames can overflow the sum. The first reads batch, the second undecompressible, and the census and the summary count 1, the number of rows saying so. The position is read off the block's first token, not written as a constant. A build without lz4 reads both as undecompressible, which the README says.

Round 3012.decision_summary: This round answers two consumer claims about the analyzer documents. First, a 64-bit integer that a document reads off the wire or a clock is a bare number up to 2^53 - 1 and the same digits in a string beyond it: a reader on doubles loses the low bits above 2^53 and one on int64 falls back to its default above 2^63, and both do it silently. One door (json::u64_into) serves the field tree, the ids and solicited_by of the census and the summary, the sequence gap sum and the retention instant; the revisions are fields 23, census 16, summary 5 and retention 2, and the gap sum now saturates instead of overflowing. Second, the two carried_state words no tracked capture produced now have one each: a compression session with one intact batch and one whose lz4 match offset is overwritten, and one fragmented Push read with and without its handshake. Both are graded by oracles the provenance gate runs. Item 809 is paid.

The platform-macos and platform-windows reasons take the hosted result as new paragraphs, assembled as the old text plus the paragraph and read back byte for byte. The reasons keep their PARTIAL tag.

The serial test. The pty arms no longer drain a pty, because a macOS pty pair shares one queue and both ends draining at once deadlock across threads; each end of the pair also runs on a task of its own. The product is unchanged and at parity with upstream's serial link.
Round 3014.decision_summary: This round reads the first hosted Platform runs after about six hours in which no hosted job started, and settles what the macOS and Windows legs can witness. The macOS leg passes all eleven targets, the pty serial arm among them. Multicast was measured on the runners before any wz code ran. On macOS a send to the group fails with no route to host unpinned and on the real interface, and works over loopback: that is the OS's local-network privacy, and upstream would be refused identically. On Windows the real interface works and loopback cannot carry multicast. So one narrow test, wz's own two drivers on one host, witnesses the host-specific plane (macOS over loopback), passes on both hosts, and becomes a gated plane target of the leg; the fuller scouting suite is intermittent on Windows and stays an observation. The Platform lane lost its Linux job, which had queued behind CI. Multicast over a real interface is not provable on a hosted macOS runner.
verification_bullets: Hosted, each job downloaded and read to the end of its log: the Platform run that followed the stall and the one after it. macOS passed all eleven targets in both, and the witness in the second; Windows passed all nine targets in both and the witness in the second, with the publish/subscribe suite passing in every run. The operating system's answers reproduced on a second macOS runner: unpinned and real-interface sends fail, loopback works.

Windows scouting across three hosted runs passed six of six, then four of six, then five of six, a different test failing each time; one of those runs executed the suite one test at a time. That is why the suite is an observation and not a gate.

On the build host, on the tree before the plane, the reason corrections and this entry were committed: the serial target passes 12 of 12 with the undrained arms, the witness passes with its final port, the reduced-feature, non-default-feature and workspace-check gates pass for the crate, and the round-fed list, the directly-called hook gates and the count guard reported no failure once the port was repaired. The plane's own selftest and check pass, and the store gates and validate-workspace pass after the reason corrections.

Not measured: the gated plane in a hosted leg, since this push is the first to carry it; the whole preflight over the tree that carries the plane and this entry, which runs before the push; multicast over a real interface on macOS, which no hosted runner can do; the cause of the Windows scouting failures beyond the operating system's interface selection; and the hosted CI run, which has sat queued behind an older one.

changes_bullets: The harness. The integration crate library gates by host what it cannot compile elsewhere: the multicast TTL reader, the opening-segment TOS reader and the window-scale reader are Linux only, the control-message walk and the two datagram and listener TOS helpers are Unix only, and the receive-buffer bound is a no-op that says so on other hosts. The two tests that use the Linux-only readers carry the same gate. The binary locators for the demo and the router add the host's executable suffix, and a router built another way is still named with the override variable.

The Windows capture. Reading a captured file positionally uses the host's call on each platform. On Windows that call moves the file cursor, and the tests give the child a duplicate of the same handle, so one cursor is shared; the read size is therefore one mebibyte on Windows so that a capture is read to its end in a single call, and the comment states what breaks if a capture ever outgrows it. This is a mitigation and not a design: a capture primitive that does not share a cursor is carried.

The scouting experiment. On Windows the six sockets the scouting tests send foreign datagrams from take the multicast egress that a route lookup returns, because the failing send in the moved-group test's control arm is one of those sockets and not wz. It is an experiment that only a Windows runner can judge, stated as one in the code, and it is reverted if an arm that passes today breaks.
The corrections. The ci.yml comment and the acknowledgement row for the cancelled validate job no longer say a cold run could not finish once; the following run was cold and passed.

The pico C build is not the obstacle. The macOS pico C ABI port is a product finding of its own and is not needed for this subset: the missing libc calls, the pthread attribute size, and the size assertion. Read the Windows scouting result for the sender change.
changes_bullets: The measurement. Platform run on the Round 3017 push, both host legs green, interop job on each host: the demo builds, the router builds, the harness does not compile. The macOS errors are in the pico C ABI crate: a libc function and a pthread function that macOS lacks, a type mismatch, and a compile-time size assertion on the task attribute (macOS's is larger than the 56 bytes asserted). The Windows errors are in the runtime's POSIX shared-memory module, which is gated on a feature the corpus crate's dev-dependency list switches on, and in the pico C build, where CMake passes MSBuild a verbatim path (the extended-length prefix) to source files that exist, and MSBuild reports them missing. The harness library itself, gated in Round 3017, is not among them.

The design change. Round 3017 first called a new crate unnecessary, on counting the library's Unix-only functions. That was right about the library and wrong about the graph: the library compiles, and the crate still cannot be built, because gating piecemeal in the product crates the dev-dependencies pull would be a port of the pico C ABI crate to macOS and of the shared-memory module to Windows, neither of which the host-owed subset needs. wz-host-interop-tests is a workspace member that depends on the corpus crate as a library only, so Cargo builds that crate's ordinary dependencies and not its dev-dependencies, and the harness stays one implementation.

The first test. wz_client_reaches_established_against_a_stock_zenohd_on_this_host has the assertion of the corpus's first router test, on purpose, and is opt-in. It passed on the build machine against the pinned router built there and the demo built there, in 0.15 seconds. The corpus keeps its copy and its count guard unchanged; when the new test has run green twice on each host the right move is to take it out of the corpus file and lower the guard in the same commit.
The Platform interop job now compiles and runs this crate, and its path filter names both crates.
Round 3018.decision_summary: This round reads the second router-interop measurement and changes where the host-owed tests live. The harness library, gated last round, no longer fails on either host; the compile now stops in the library's dependencies. On macOS the pico C ABI crate uses Linux-only calls and a pthread attribute size that differs. On Windows the runtime's POSIX shared-memory module has no Windows spelling, and the pico C build hands MSBuild a verbatim path it cannot open. All of that is reached only because the corpus crate lists those crates as dev-dependencies, and a dev-dependency is built for every test target of its package, including the one test that needs none of them. So the host-owed tests move to a crate of their own that uses the corpus crate as a library, which brings in its ordinary dependencies only. The first test, the demo reaching Established against a stock router, passes on Linux against the pinned router.
verification_bullets: Hosted, each job read to its verdict lines and its first compiler errors: the Platform run on the Round 3017 push. Both legs passed; on each host the interop job printed demo PASS, harness FAIL, router PASS, handshake SKIPPED. The CI run before it carried the job split and passed both new jobs, with one job still running when read.

Add the macOS-only Unix socket row, with the demo's unixsock feature built on macOS alone, and a gate that derives the rows from the platform matrix: for every link the pin serves on a host and the default router build serves too, there is a test in the host crate or a listed gap with its reason.
Decide how the corpus keeps its copies: when a host test has two green runs per host, take its twin out of the corpus file and lower the corpus lane's count guard in the same commit.

Replace the Windows capture mitigation with a primitive that does not share a cursor, make the router builder script host-portable, and read the Windows scouting result for the sender change over more runs.
changes_bullets: The evidence. On macOS the demo connected to the router at a loopback address over tcp, logged session Established and emitted five Put pushes, and the test finished in 0.41 seconds; on Windows the same, in 0.19 seconds. The shared-cursor mitigation of Round 3017, a one mebibyte read to the end of the capture, was exercised on Windows by a real test for the first time and held. The router built by cargo install took about three and a half minutes on macOS and seven on Windows.

The measurement that sets the subset. The corpus classifier, which resolves each test's call graph to the foreign programs it can reach, gives 652 tests, of which 83 reach only the router. Reading the router file shows why that is not the host's subset: its eight router-only tests are the handshake over each link plus two mesh dials over a Unix socket, and the files beside it that reach only the router test configuration reading, adminspace queries and gossip, which no host changes. The host-dependent surface of a transport is its links, so a host owes the interop over each link it serves.

The rows. A table-driven test file in the host crate carries one row per link, WebSocket, UDP, TLS and QUIC, with one shared body and one test function per link, so that two consecutive green runs are counted per link and a red names its link. The certificate links take their material from the existing test-support fixture. The Platform interop job builds the demo with the three link features and prints one verdict line per link.
Left out, each with its reason: a Unix socket is served on macOS only, so it is a row macOS alone owes; unixpipe and vsock need a router built with a transport feature the default build omits.
Round 3019.decision_summary: This round records the first router interop evidence from a macOS and a Windows host, and fixes what the rest of the host-owed subset is. The Platform run on the Round 3018 push, read to the end of both interop jobs: on each host the demo builds, the new crate's tests compile, the pinned router builds, and the demo reaches Established against it over TCP, in under half a second. That is one green run per host, so the test stays an observation; the owner's rule needs two consecutive. The subset is not the 83 of 652 corpus tests that reach only the router, because most of those test logic no host changes. What a host owes is the router interop over each link it serves, which is the surface the platform matrix already derives, and the corpus has exactly one pure handshake per link. The crate gains the WebSocket, UDP, TLS and QUIC rows, one test each.
verification_bullets: Hosted, each interop job read to its four verdict lines and to the test's own output: the Platform run on the Round 3018 push. Both legs passed. macOS and Windows each printed demo PASS, host interop tests compile PASS, router PASS, handshake PASS, and the captured demo output shows the connection, the Established line and the Put emission.

On the build machine: the four link tests pass against the pinned router and a demo built with the ws, tls and quic features, 0.62 seconds, each asserting the demo's own log of the transport it dialed; the crate formats and the lock file resolves offline.

Not measured: the four link rows on either host, which the next interop run reads; a second consecutive green run of the TCP handshake on either host, without which it stays an observation; the Windows scouting result beyond the one run recorded in the last round; and the whole preflight over the tree that carries this entry, which runs before the push.

carry_forward_bullets: Read the next Platform run per host: the gating step's line (promoted tests passed, expected one), and the first observations of reliable UDP and QUIC datagram on both hosts and of the Unix socket on macOS. Beyond the handshake: the host-dependent surface of a link is also its data plane. The corpus has a data-plane test per link that needs the pico C library as the subscriber; a pico-free subscriber for the host crate (the demo itself, as a second client) would let each link carry a Put and not only reach Established.

changes_bullets: The evidence. The Platform run on the Round 3019 push, each interop job read to its verdict lines and to the tests' own output. macOS: the TCP handshake passed in 0.42 seconds, and WebSocket, UDP, TLS and QUIC each passed in about half a second, every one logging the transport the demo dialed. Windows: the same five lines passed. That is the second consecutive green run of the TCP handshake on each host (the first was the run before), so it is promoted on both; each link row has one green run per host.

The rows built instead of registered. Reliable UDP is the udp scheme with a reliability query value on the router's listener and on the demo's locator; QUIC datagram is the quic scheme with the datagram query value on the router, and a scheme of its own on the demo. Neither needs a router built with an extra feature, so neither is a debt. A Unix socket row exists for macOS alone, behind cfg(unix), with the demo's unixsock feature built only there. The seven link tests pass on the build machine against the pinned router and the demo built with all the link features; the crate compiles for the Windows and macOS targets with warnings denied.

The gate. A fifth arm of the platform matrix gate. INTEROP maps a link kind to its test; INTEROP_GAPS holds the links the default router does not serve (serial on both hosts, unixpipe on macOS), with one reason that the gate checks against the pin's default feature list, so a router that gains a link turns its row into a finding; every opt-in test of the host crate must be named by the table. INTEROP_PROMOTED holds the two run ids that earned each promotion. A promoted test must be run by a step of the Platform interop job that is not continue-on-error, found in the workflow's text because the gate runs on hosts with no YAML reader, and the list that step runs is printed by --promoted HOST, so the workflow holds no second copy. The selftest drives every verdict, and two mutants of the real workflow, the gating step made continue-on-error and a link dropped from the job's list, are each caught on the real tree.

The gating step. The job reads the promoted list, runs each test with --ignored against the router the observation step built, and refuses a run that selected no passing test, because a name carrying the carriage return Python writes on Windows selects nothing and cargo calls that a pass.
Round 3020.decision_summary: This round reads the second hosted run of the host router interop and turns what it showed into rules. The two links that looked like debts, reliable UDP and QUIC datagram, are variants of a scheme the stock router serves (a query value on the same scheme), so they became rows instead and pass against the pinned router on the build machine. The platform matrix gate gains a fifth arm: every link wz serves on a host has an interop test or a row saying the default router omits it, checked against the pin's own default feature list, and a promoted test must be run by a step that can fail the job. Promotion is therefore a mechanism, not a word.

carry_forward_bullets: Read the next Platform run: the pin step's line, the gating step's line (five promoted tests per host expected), and the second green of reliable UDP and QUIC datagram on both hosts and of the Unix socket on macOS. changes_bullets: The evidence. The Platform run on the Round 3020 push, both interop jobs read to every verdict line and to the tests' own output. macOS: the router built, eight tests passed (TCP, WebSocket, UDP, reliable UDP, TLS, QUIC, QUIC datagram, Unix socket) and the gating step reported one promoted test passed. changes_bullets: The answer to the owner. The C ABI gap on macOS and Windows is not physical; the physical limits are a real tty, multicast over a real interface and a COM port, which a hosted runner cannot show. Registering the C ABI as a debt row was a scoping choice and not a necessity, and the row says what closes it.

The macOS port. The pico C ABI crate's four compile errors are fixed. Random bytes are drawn with arc4random_buf where pico's macOS arm does; the condvar skips the clock attribute macOS lacks and waits on an interval from the monotonic clock with the Darwin-only relative wait, as pico does; the microseconds of a wall time are widened, since their type is 64 bits on Linux and 32 on macOS; and the task attribute size, the one assertion that failed, is a per-host pin, 56 bytes on Linux and 64 on macOS, read off Darwin's layout. The interval arithmetic is a pure function with a unit test on every host. The crate is clippy-clean with warnings denied for the Linux and the macOS targets, its 83 unit tests pass on Linux, and the full rustdoc budget lane passes.

The measurements. Against each target, source only, with the C build steps stubbed: on macOS the zenoh-c crate and the neutral core compile unchanged; on Windows the zenoh-c crate and the neutral core compile, as do the runtime and the session core, and the pico C ABI crate has 42 errors in two files, every one a POSIX name it calls through libc. pico's own Windows layer types its mutex as SRWLOCK, its recursive mutex as CRITICAL_SECTION, its condvar as CONDITION_VARIABLE, its clock as LARGE_INTEGER and its wall time as the C runtime's timeb, so the Windows port is a Win32 implementation of those exports over those types.

The correction. The debt row written in Round 3023 said the Windows C ABI is blocked by the runtime's shared-memory module. That is the corpus crate's problem through its dev-dependency list and is not on the C ABI's path. The row, and the two platform reasons, take a correction paragraph each, assembled as the old text plus the paragraph and read back byte for byte; their tags and claims do not move.

changes_bullets: The pico C program. A C file compiled against zenoh-pico's own headers for the host, with the generated config the vendored library's build installs, and linked to the wz library instead of libzenohpico, drives the mutex, condition variable, task, clock, wall time and random exports the way pico's examples do. Each value of a pico type sits between guard bytes, so a layout that is wrong is caught where it writes; a control hands a one-byte value to an export that initialises a mutex and must trip the guard. On macOS the compiler is cc, on Windows it is MSVC's cl through the Visual Studio environment, because pico's Windows header names an inline function __asm__, a keyword to a GNU-mode compiler. It opens no session.

The Windows layouts. A step asks clang, over the Windows SDK headers, for sizeof of the five types pico's Windows backend uses and compares the line with the one the Rust test prints for its own types. Two consecutive runs read it equal, so it lost its continue-on-error.

The vendored library on Windows. Three things stood between the pico C library and a Windows host, found one at a time by the runs: the CMake path was the verbatim form MSBuild rejects, so the build script now asks dunce; the build script had no platform macro for a Windows target, so the mapping moved to a tested module and gained one; and clang, which bindgen runs, reads pico's header function named __asm__ as a keyword, which MSVC does not, so the parse renames it. Each was reproduced or read before it was fixed: the first in a hosted log, the third with clang locally, with and without the rename.
The crate's own header. It declared the Unix clock type on every host; it now declares the 8-byte counter union on Windows, checked under both shapes with a size assertion and a control that fails.

The lane's build was reproduced on this host with its normalised flags for four trees: the previous green tree 64048 (hosted 64056), the same tree with only the SCE pin moved 64192, the pushed tree 64192, and the receive-path change below 64180. The pin accounts for all of the growth, +144 here and +140 hosted, and the Put codec's new chain identifier for none of it. A per-symbol diff of the old-pin and new-pin images names it: +102 bytes in the statechart engine's microstep procedures, one instance per statechart the image carries, +18 in the entry function that absorbs the rest, +12 and +6 in two small functions, and anonymous constants that changed only their hash. The receive path. A transport Frame's payload is now the bytes it was decoded from as a range of the unit and not a copy of it, through a decode that is handed the unit itself. The drive loop makes the unit shareable once, before anything is decoded: a lent buffer stays as it is and an owned read is moved behind one reference count, which costs one allocation and no copy. The batch walk then decodes into messages that hold ranges of that storage, a remainder of a batch that is parked for the next turn is a range of it too, and a completed reassembly chain, which exists only as a borrowed slot, is copied once into a buffer of its own and walked from there, so the bytes moved are the same as before and no message holds a slice of a slot that is about to be reused.

The Sample. A sample's payload is the shareable bytes type and no longer a vector. The registry projects a received Put into a sample by taking the message's payload field as it is, and the view of a sample answers its payload as shareable bytes, so the owned sample the session builds for every user callback, and any sample an application keeps, is a second reference to the frame's storage. Holding a sample keeps the frame's pool slot out of the pool until it is dropped, which is the declared meaning of the atom. A sliced Put is still assembled from its slices and is a new buffer.

The witnesses. Six tests drive a real established session: a lent unit, a heap unit, the remainder of a batch, a subscriber's callback, an application's kept sample read by the count of holders of the lent storage, and a control that the copying decode owns its payload. One more reads the node's own receive pool: a sample kept from a pool frame is bytes of the slot, and the slot stays out of the freelist until the sample drops. A reassembly test reads that a slice-only batch is decoded into one lent copy. Each was reddened by the copy it replaced and by nothing else: the drive decoding over a copy reddens three legs, leaving a heap unit owned reddens two, parking the remainder as a copy reddens one, the reassembly copying walk reddens its test, the registry projection copying reddens the callback leg, and the retention copying reddens the kept-sample leg and the pool test.

Round 3051.decision_summary: This round measures the router hop, which every earlier leg skipped. Each wz-to-zenoh leg dialled the upstream program directly, so whether a descriptor wz wrote survives a router, which reads the message, maps the buffer and writes it again, had no answer. Upstream's shared-memory zenohd is put between the two ends in three legs: a wz publisher to z_sub_shm, z_pub_shm to a wz subscriber, and a wz getter's value to z_queryable_shm. All three crossed as shared memory: the far subscriber printed wz's payload as a shared-memory buffer, wz's resolver was asked for each of the publisher's descriptors and refused none, and the queryable printed the getter's value as SHM. The raw control, a wz that offers no shared memory, was handed the same samples with the resolver never asked. Nothing in wz changed; the answer is that the layout wz writes and reads already survives a re-serialising router.

changes_bullets: The seam. A new module holds the value types an allocation speaks in (alignment, layout, chunk descriptor, the two error types, a pointer that owns its segment) and the backend trait: allocate, free, defragment, available, layout_for, and a protocol id. They are upstream's types field for field, because the C ABI above exposes them one for one.

The pool. The built-in backend is one POSIX segment with a first-fit free list over it and neighbours coalesced on release. It answers 0 to available and defragment and reports out of memory for a request it cannot serve, as the source of upstream's default backend does.

The provider. ShmProvider draws a metadata slot per chunk, writes the header a receiver follows (segment, offset, length, protocol), keeps the chunk on its own busy list, and takes it back when the count reads zero: the slot goes stale, the memory goes back to the backend, the slot rejoins the queue. Four allocation policies compose as runtime values. A provider with no handle left is collected by the process, on an allocation and on the watchdog tick.
ShmBackedPayload::alloc is a provider whose pool is one payload; its callers, the session paths and the resolver are unchanged. The metadata store no longer owns a busy list.

Pins. The cross-implementation audit counts one more adjudicated link, the lane that runs the interop file expects seven legs, and the provider lane's count is 32 with a second guard of 15 for the two new modules.
Round 3056.decision_summary: Round 3056 gives the runtime the shape of upstream's shared-memory provider, which is the base under the C ABI's sending half and under the pool residual transport-shm has carried since R2862. A payload used to be a data segment of its own, created for it and unlinked with it, so there was no memory for a second chunk to share. Now a backend allocates chunks of a pool segment, and a provider draws a metadata slot per chunk, keeps it on a busy list, and gives the memory back only when the reference count reads zero. The old single payload is a provider whose pool is one payload, so no caller changed. Upstream's own subscriber reads two chunks of one segment at offsets 0 and 16, each with its own bytes.

It publishes the two chunks of a 32-byte pool and z_sub_shm prints each chunk's own bytes as a shared-memory buffer, the headers naming one segment at offsets 0 and 16; a live provider still holds both after their owners let go; once zenoh has released them a collection takes them home, both descriptors go stale and the whole pool is one chunk again.

Three runs of the corrected row against the real library and wz are green. A set comparison is still red for a Hello that lists one locator, which is what the first mutation of Round 3076 produced; that mutation was not run again.

The static gates, the cross-impl audit, the rustdoc budget and Layer C1cc whole are run again on the committed tree after this entry and read from their own exit codes; the layer stops at its first failure, so twenty of its fifty-five legs had not run when the Hello row failed.

carry_forward_bullets: The macro against the function tells a consumer whether it linked the library its header describes, but nothing makes a consumer ask; that stays the consumer's, and the header now says how.
The sentinel's agreement with the dissect record's is held by a test in this library and not by the other library; if that crate's sentinel moves, this crate's test is what says so.
changes_bullets: The replay header carries the ABI revision as a macro beside the function that reports it, and a new gate reads the define, loads the built library, calls the function and refuses on a disagreement; its selftest holds the reader to the define, so a prose mention of the macro cannot answer for it.

The no-timestamp comment now states that only the sentinel is shared with the dissect record's timestamp, that the units differ (milliseconds against nanoseconds), and the conversion: divide a real reading and pass the sentinel through undivided.
The C consumer and the replay vocabulary gate follow the macro, and three tests in the replay crate pin the conversion, the two unit slips nothing refuses, and the macro against the function.
Round 3078.decision_summary: This round answers two things a consumer found the replay header leaving open. The ABI revision existed only as a function, so a build linked against a library it was not compiled for had no way to see the difference; the header now also carries it as a macro beside the function, and a gate loads the built library, calls the function and refuses when the two differ. And the no-timestamp comment said the sentinel is the same number as the dissect record's, which reads as "a record's timestamp can be fed straight in"; it cannot, because a replay time is milliseconds and a record's is nanoseconds. The comment now says only the sentinel is shared, gives the conversion, and tests hold it, including the two slips nothing refuses. The revision does not move: a define is compiled in, not linked.
verification_bullets: Layer C1cj builds the cdylib, loads it, compares the macro with what it reports and compiles the C consumer against the header; it passed in the final verification run, as did the replay vocabulary gate and the rest of the static gates the pre-push hook defers, run in one pass with none stopping the others.

The three new tests ran in the changed-crate test pass of the extended pre-push sweep, which passed end to end: the mandatory gates, the gate list, Layer 0, a changed gate's own selftest, the crate tests, the doc links, the reduced and non-default feature builds and the workspace type check.
Not mutation-tested: no break was put into the conversion or the new gate to see the tests go red.

carry_forward_bullets: The shim's interface table holds two, which is what a board with two links needs and no more; a third interface is refused by name and not grown.
The default route follows the first gateway added, so a node that wants the second link's gateway as its route must add that link first, and nothing yet lets it say so.
changes_bullets: EthernetMac and the frame bound move to the dependency-free trait tier, the LAN9118 chip becomes its own crate, the lwIP link crate re-exports the seam under its old paths, and the MCU admin node names the chip crate it drives.

The lwIP shim gives the default route only to the first interface added with a non-zero gateway and never moves it; EthernetIf reports whether it holds the route, and the lwIP test harness empties the interface table between tests.
Two interfaces on two networks are tested apart, each with its own cable and far host, so the order they are added in cannot decide a route.
Round 3079.decision_summary: This round makes the first Ethernet MAC a crate of its own and makes a node with two interfaces route correctly. The LAN9118 driver lived inside the lwIP link crate, so a board with another MAC would have had to carry lwIP's; the MAC trait and the frame bound now sit in the dependency-free trait tier, the chip is its own crate, and the link crate re-exports the seam under its old paths so no caller moved. Making a second interface possible exposed that every interface added to lwIP took the default route, so the last one added won whatever gateways they had: the first interface added with a gateway now holds the route, a later one never moves it, and one with no gateway is on-link only. Two interfaces are tested apart.
verification_bullets: Three breaks of the route rule, each applied alone, were each caught by the lwIP link crate's tests: the gateway ignored, a later gateway taking the route, and every interface taking it as before.

Layer Qa, which runs the lwIP admin node on QEMU over the LAN9118 crate against a stock router, passed all six steps on the final tree: the GET before a write, a PUT that makes the node dial, the written config, the link ends, the status document and a refused group.
The changed-crate tests, doc links and non-default feature clippy for the crates this round touched passed in the extended pre-push sweep.

carry_forward_bullets: The shell runs on lwIP (Layer Qa) and, with the next round, on Zephyr's sockets (Layer Qza); there is no third stack, so its stack-neutrality beyond those two rests on the in-memory network.
The in-memory network is a test network and not a transport: it has no loss, reordering or timing, and a test that needs them needs another model.
changes_bullets: A new shell crate holds the application layer, the admin node, the connection manager and the dialer, depends on no link crate, and runs on the SessionLinks seam of the cooperative runtime; the lwIP crate keeps its links and re-exports the shell under its old paths.

An in-memory network is the shell's test network: it refuses a second bind of a port, frees the port when an end is dropped, lets an acceptor learn its peer from the first datagram, steps over taken ephemeral ports and wraps round at the last one.

The surface census and the feature test census take the new crate (an axis-reach row, and a hook-scope row naming the features that reach its seventeen feature-gated tests), and the C1m lane counts five shell legs and the lwIP crate's, each number the one its own run printed.
Round 3080.decision_summary: This round makes the MCU session shell a crate that names no network stack. The application layer, the admin node, the connection manager and the dialer lived in the lwIP session crate and could be reached only over lwIP, which made "the admin node works" and "the admin node works on lwIP" one claim. They are now their own crate, generic over what a stack gives them: a link that accepts on a port and a link that dials an address, a seam in the cooperative runtime. The lwIP half stays in the lwIP crate and is re-exported under its old paths. The shell is tested on an in-memory network that is no stack's, so lwIP and Zephyr's sockets each have only to show that their own links satisfy the seam.
verification_bullets: Fourteen breaks of the shell and its network were put in alone: the node never listening again, an old session kept while binding, declarations never forgotten, declared on every tick, declared before the session is established, sessions not reported, an exhausted dial taken for a refusal, a dial as acceptor, the established flag forgotten, a port bound twice, a dropped end keeping its port, a peer not learnt, taken ephemeral ports not skipped, and no wrap. All fourteen were caught, after four gaps were closed with tests: the relisten in the order a firmware loop really has, the established guard, the ephemeral stepping and wrap, and lwIP's bind refusal.
Layer C1m passed (the eighteen count legs and the clippy legs of both crates), and Layer Qa passed all six steps with the shell running on lwIP.
The extended pre-push sweep passed; the feature test census, which found seventeen of the shell's tests run by no leg, passes with its row.

carry_forward_bullets: The peak was measured over this scenario; a peer that sends something it does not could go deeper, which is why a quarter is left free and why the node keeps reporting a new peak. The stack's depth is the largest remaining cost of polling every session inline, and nothing yet reduces it.
The lwIP backend on the T2G board shares the 32 KiB stack; its depth has not been measured on silicon, and the node will print it there.
A station address drawn at boot takes the node's zenoh id with it, so a node that must keep its identity across a reboot is built with the explicit source.
changes_bullets: ZephyrLinks accepts and dials over Zephyr's BSD sockets; board hooks give the address and the id, one image macro writes the allocator, the critical section and the panic handler, and const parsers read tick rate, address and MAC from the board's build.

A shared Zephyr module derives the Rust target, tick rate and entropy from Kconfig; the admin node runs over Zephyr's stack or over lwIP on a MAC crate and advertises every interface; the station address is drawn at boot or given with a build option, with no shared default.

The node prints stack: peak N of M bytes from the kernel's painted stack, its main stack is 32 KiB with a sentinel that makes an overflow a named fatal error, and Layer Qza refuses a missing line and a peak that leaves under a quarter free.
Round 3081.decision_summary: This round puts the admin node on Zephyr over whatever stack the board has, and makes the board an argument of the image. Zephyr's sockets are a SessionLinks provider (bind reads back the port it chose, so a dialled session can name its link), the images take their Rust target, tick rate and entropy from the board's Kconfig, and fixture entropy is admitted on a QEMU board only. The station address is drawn at boot unless one is given: no value every build shares can be right for two boards on one network, and the chip's HAL has no per-unit identifier. Layer Qza then found the node dead after its first session: its 16 KiB main stack was one the node needs 20,012 bytes of, and it ran into the idle thread's below it. The node now measures its own stack and Qza refuses a peak over three quarters.
verification_bullets: Layer Qza passed all eight steps against a stock router on QEMU: the node's console, a GET, a PUT that makes it dial, the written config, the link ends, the status document, a refused group of two, and the stack margin. The node's own line read peak 20048 of 32768 bytes.

The fault was read off the halted machine with a debugger and not guessed at: the exception frame belonged to the idle thread, the main stack's bounds and the words at its low end showed it had run to its bottom, and a 64 KiB painted stack measured the peak at 20,012 bytes.

The stack check was shown to refuse: a 24 KiB stack and an image that no longer measures its stack each failed Qza at the step that names them, and the node's configuration file was restored byte for byte.
Twelve breaks of the const parsers, the clock conversion and the entropy and epoch hooks were all caught; the crate's host tests are twelve and Layer C1ns counts them. Layers Qz, Qzb and C1ns passed.

carry_forward_bullets: The T2G Ethernet is BUILT. The pins come from the kit's board support package and the PDL's pin table for this device, the MAC from the PDL's block, and none of it has run on silicon; HARDWARE needs a lab's record in the store.
The PHY's address is found by scan; the kit's schematic was not read for it, and a scan that finds the wrong device on a board with two would say nothing.
changes_bullets: The CYT4BF MAC crate drives the MXETH block through a Board trait and is host-tested against a model of the controller that follows the wrap flag as the hardware does; its PHY half scans for a clause 22 PHY, resets it, starts negotiation and applies the agreed speed and duplex.

The T2G image's lwIP backend, pin routing and TRNG hook build for the kit; a QEMU lane for the admin node and a table-driven build lane are new, and a gate with red-first fixtures reads the board table and refuses a claim above its evidence.

The rows are QEMU for the two images on the an385 board, BUILT for the T2G Ethernet row, and DECLARED for the 10BASE-T1S row with its reason; HARDWARE rows need a full record and a store entry that exists.
Round 3082.decision_summary: This round gives the T2G kit its Ethernet and says how far each claim about it goes. The CYT4BF family's MAC is a crate of its own: a Cadence GEM, polled, one descriptor ring each way, with a clause 22 PHY found by scan and its negotiated mode applied, and the admin node's lwIP backend drives it with the chip's own TRNG as the session's entropy. A table of boards, one row for each board, link and application, says how far each is witnessed: DECLARED, BUILT, QEMU or HARDWARE. A claim goes no higher than the lowest grade its evidence reaches, a gate holds every row to its evidence, and Layer Qzb builds every BUILT row. The T2G row is BUILT and nothing here has run on silicon; HARDWARE needs a lab's record.
verification_bullets: Nine breaks of the MAC were put in alone: the receive and transmit wrap flags at init and at send, a full ring ignored, the transmit pointer not rewritten on recovery, a fatal transmit status not recovered, a down link still transmitting, the end-of-frame flag not required, and receive overrun not cleared. All nine were caught after the model was made to follow the wrap flag: the break at send had survived because the model wrapped the ring by arithmetic and never noticed the flag was gone.
The PHY double's tests now assert how many registers it was read for, which the test double gate demanded: without it a refusal could be the fixture's and not the code's.
Layer Qzb built both BUILT rows, the board table gate and its selftest passed, Layer C0 passed all 192 of its legs, and the extended pre-push sweep passed.

carry_forward_bullets: No chip crate exists and the chip is not identified: the one board that could carry a T1S device carries it only as an expansion board, which the kit's user guide does not name. The identity probe of the next round is how a lab learns it.
The model is written from the interface as one driver lays it out; a real chip may differ from it, and that is what a hardware record would show.
changes_bullets: SpiTransfer joins EthernetMac in the trait tier: one call is one chip-select assertion, full duplex, tx and rx the same length.

A new TC6 crate does control reads and writes with the parity and the protected mode, data chunk exchanges, the standard registers, and the chunking and reassembly of frames in the receive mode where a frame starts on a chunk boundary.
Its twenty-five host tests run it against a model of a TC6 chip, with a footer builder that now carries the start word offset.
Round 3083.decision_summary: This round writes the OPEN Alliance 10BASE-T1x serial interface (TC6) as a protocol and nothing of any chip. A TC6 MAC-PHY is a whole Ethernet controller behind four SPI wires, and the interface is the same for every chip that implements it: control transactions with header parity and the protected mode, data chunk exchanges with transmit credits and receive chunk counts, the chunking of a frame each way and the reassembly of a received one. It runs over a new SpiTransfer seam in the dependency-free trait tier and is presented as an EthernetMac, so a chip crate on top has only its own registers to write. It is BUILT: no emulator models a TC6 chip, so the tests drive it against a model written from the same reading of the interface.
verification_bullets: Thirteen breaks of the protocol were put in alone: the parity bit inverted and the parity check inverted, a footer's parity unchecked, a rejected header and a lost sync ignored, the credit check skipped and its re-ask skipped, the drop flag ignored, a frame start off a chunk boundary accepted, a chunk of a frame never started accepted, a frame past the limit not refused, extended status not cleared after a send, and the end offset zero. All thirteen were caught, after three gaps were closed with a footer start-offset field and three tests.
The changed-crate tests, doc links and non-default feature clippy passed in the extended pre-push sweep, and Layer C0 passed.

carry_forward_bullets: The master and the probe are BUILT. A lab with the expansion board builds the overlay and reads two lines at boot; that is the first record, and it names the chip. A chip crate waits for that name.
The probe's mode (0) is how Zephyr's TC6 chip driver opens its device, and its rate (1 MHz) is a probe's, under any chip's limit; a chip crate chooses its own.
The socket's interrupt pin was read off a figure in the user guide and not out of the board support package, and must be checked against the board when the chip crate is written.
changes_bullets: A new SCB rules crate holds the rate arithmetic, the four SPI modes, the exchange limits and an SpiTransfer adapter over a ScbMaster trait that the board implements.

A thin C driver on the PDL runs SCB3 with a clock divider it finds free, the kit's pin routing names SCB3 and slave select line 2, and an overlay turns on the boot-time read of the two identity registers; Zephyr's own SPI binding is not used, because it requires an interrupts property the SoC's SCB nodes lack.
The board table gains a BUILT row for the probe image, and the 10BASE-T1S row is rewritten to say what is known: the chip is unidentified and is an expansion board, not a device of the kit.
Round 3084.decision_summary: This round builds what a TC6 chip needs of the board that does not depend on which chip it is: an SPI master on the T2G kit's MikroBUS socket. The rules of an SCB-based master are the same on every board, so they are a host-tested crate: a requested rate becomes a divider and an oversample factor from the clock the chip actually has, taking the fastest pair not above the target; an exchange is one chip-select assertion no longer than the 128-byte FIFO, because the block releases chip select when the FIFO runs dry and an exchange that did not fit would be cut in two; and an adapter enforces both. The registers are the PDL's, called from a thin C driver that finds a free clock divider instead of naming one. An image option reads the two TC6 identity registers at boot, which is how a lab learns the chip.
verification_bullets: Twelve breaks of the rate rule, the exchange rules and the mode bits were put in alone (the tie rule, the oversample order, the rounding, the divider limit, a zero target, the FIFO's size refused or exceeded, an empty or mismatched exchange allowed, the two mode bits swapped, a board error hidden); all twelve were caught by the crate's seven tests.
Layer Qzb built the probe image through the PDL and the kit's pins, which is the first evidence that the C driver compiles and links; nothing has run on an SCB.
The extended pre-push sweep passed.

carry_forward_bullets: The chip's product and silicon revision stay unknown until DEVID is read on the bench. The chip crate waits for that, and must refuse a revision whose configuration is not documented instead of applying another revision's.

The M7 image still needs a CM0+ image that configures the clock tree and starts CM7_0, and wz ships none. Next: a launcher image for the CM0+ core, a boot-time check of the core clock against the build's assumption so that a wrong clock stops the node with one line, and bounds on the PHY waits by elapsed time instead of by the delays requested.
The link path has not been seen to run to its end; the lab is capturing a boot for minutes with the new lines.
The probe row stays BUILT: the lab reported the image's hash prefix and two of the three registers, but no verdict grammar exists for the row and DEVID was not yet read.
changes_bullets: The probe reads the LAN8650/1's DEVID (memory map selector 10, address 0x0094) beside the two standard registers and logs its model and revision fields.
The T2G bring-up prints a line at each step (pins routed, MAC initialised, link bring-up returned) with the kernel's own uptime, so a bench can set it against a wall clock.
The board table records, on the three T2G rows, what the first boot showed, the CM0+ image that the clock tree and the start of CM7_0 depend on, and what is and is not known of the chip.
Round 3085.decision_summary: The first boot of the T2G probe image with a 10BASE-T1S click plugged in gave this stack its first facts from silicon, and they correct three things. The marking taken for a chip name was the RJ45 jack's. The standard identity register cannot name the chip: on the LAN8650/1 it reflects the integrated PHY only, as the vendor's errata state, so its reading (model 0x1B, revision 4, where the data sheets give 3) fixes the family and not the product or revision; the chip's own DEVID does, so the probe now reads it, and the driver for this chip waits for that answer. And the 100 seconds of silence was a time base, not a fault: the lab measured the core at about 8 MHz where the build assumes 350, because the clock tree is the CM0+ image's job (Zephyr's clock driver returns on the M7) and wz ships none. The bring-up now prints the kernel's uptime at each step.
verification_bullets: The register addresses, field layouts and the errata item were read as text from two revisions of the vendor's data sheet and from its errata; that OA_PHYID reflects the PHY's clause 22 identifier is the data sheet's own statement.

The lab measured the kernel's tick count against a wall clock over two intervals of 10 seconds (229.0 and 228.2 ticks per second where 10000 is configured) and the cycle counter (8.02 MHz where 350 MHz is configured); the two ratios agree at about 44.
Layer Qzb built both T2G images with the change.
The board table gate passes. The probe's two shifts have no host test; a chip crate will own the decode.

carry_forward_bullets: One job of the previous push's hosted run was still running when its failure was read; its verdict is read at the start of the next round.
The gate finds the shape by a function's name. A lookup that returns a port under another name would pass it, so the rule stays a reviewer's as well as the gate's.
changes_bullets: The in-memory network binds an ephemeral port by finding and claiming it in one step; the lookup that returned a bare port number is removed.
The initiator's open uses it, and the tests that step over taken ports, wrap round and hand out distinct ports run unchanged.
Round 3086.decision_summary: Layer C0g went red on the hosted run of the previous push. It refuses a private fn free_port outside the shared test-support crate, because a function that looks up a free port and returns it leaves a window between the lookup and the bind in which the answer goes stale. The session shell's in-memory network had one, added with the shell. The window cannot be hit there, since the network is single-threaded and the two calls are back to back, but the shape is the one the gate exists to keep out, and a rename would have passed the gate and kept the shape. So the network now has one operation that finds a port and claims it under one borrow and returns an end that already owns it, and nothing that returns a bare port number.
verification_bullets: The red was attributed from the hosted job's own log: Layer C0g, the free_port arm, naming the one definition in the shell crate; it was the only failed job of that run when read, 21 of 22 having finished.
Layer C0g passes locally with no private copy left.
The shell crate's tests pass in the default and the full-feature legs at their counts (3 and 20), and clippy with warnings denied passes on both sets.
The window was not a failure observed here: the change is for the shape the gate guards, not for a bug that fired.

carry_forward_bullets: The launcher is BUILT and has never run. It replaces the kit's CM0+ image, so flashing it is the lab's and the owner's decision; the lab has backed up the image that is there.
Whether the clock tree it brings up is what the M7_0 image needs is what the next run on the kit measures: the tick count against a wall clock.
A companion has no HARDWARE record format yet, so a row that requires one cannot be HARDWARE until it does.
Still open: the boot-time check of the core clock against the build's assumption, the PHY waits bounded by elapsed time, and the console's silence after the probe, which the clock does not explain.
changes_bullets: A CM0+ launcher image brings the clock tree up through Zephyr's own driver, checks that an M7_0 image is present, and starts the core with every wait bounded on the cycle counter.
The board table gains companions and a row's requires. Its gate refuses a row that requires an unlisted image or one graded below the row, and its selftest has nine new refusal arms.
Layer Qzb builds the companions and compares the address the launcher's build names with the address the M7_0 image's vector table is linked at.
Round 3087.decision_summary: The measurement that explained the silence also named what was missing: on a T2G chip the CM0+ core runs first and is the one that brings the clock tree up and starts the M7_0 core, Zephyr's clock driver returns without touching the tree in an M7 build, and wz shipped no CM0+ image, so an M7 image started by a CM0+ image that did neither ran at 8 MHz where it was built for 350. This round supplies the image: a launcher for the CM0+ target that lets Zephyr's own driver bring the tree up from the board's devicetree and then starts M7_0 at the start of the M7_0 flash partition, read from the same devicetree node the M7_0 image is linked at, with every wait bounded on the cycle counter. The board table learns that a row can run with other images: it lists them as companions, a row names what it requires, and a row's grade stops at the lowest grade of what it runs with. Layer Qzb builds the launcher and checks that the two images agree on the address.
verification_bullets: Layer Qzb built both M7_0 images and the launcher, and its seam check agreed on 0x10080000.

The comparison was run on fake build logs for agreement, disagreement, a build that never names an address, a missing image address and a difference of case only; it refused the three it should and passed the two it should.
Seventeen static gates that read the touched files each ended on their own passing line.
Nothing ran on a chip.

carry_forward_bullets: The transmit DMA's bus error is unexplained. The lab's reads: the first descriptor queued (length 42, last-buffer set, used clear), the frame in its buffer valid when read from the debugger, the words after it zero, every address inside the DMA section, the status bit set before any traffic and not set again once cleared, the queue pointer never moving.

The stall without a debugger is deterministic and unexplained: the cycle count at the halt was 30.2 million in two separate boots with the same tick count, and the core was running a cycle-counter read loop while the system timer was not advancing; a debugger attaching lets it go on. The chip runs on its 8 MHz oscillator with no clock tree, so that configuration is the first suspect and the launcher is the next test.

The lab may flash the launcher only with the owner's consent; it has backed up the image it would replace. After it, the stall, the transmit error and the receive path are measured again under the clock tree the M7 image was built for.
changes_bullets: The CYT4BF MAC driver clears its whole DMA area with 32-bit stores when it is constructed, before the controller is given any address in it.
The firmware's own description of the section now says it is NOLOAD and that the driver is what initialises it.
Round 3088.decision_summary: The lab's second run on the T2G kit gave facts about two failures, and one of them holds a mistake of the driver's whatever its cause. The transmit DMA stopped on a bus error at the first frame, with the descriptor queued, the frame valid and every address inside the section the DMA can reach, so the cause is not yet known. What the driver did assume, wrongly, is that its DMA area starts as zeroes: Zephyr's section for it is NOLOAD, so the zeroes the image holds are never applied and the RAM keeps what it held at reset, which on RAM with ECC can include words nothing has written. The driver now writes the whole area, a word at a time, before it points the controller at it. Whether that is what stopped the transmit DMA is not known and is not claimed: the same boots show the chip running on its 8 MHz oscillator with no clock tree, and the next measurement is made with the CM0+ launcher that brings the tree up.
verification_bullets: A new host test fills the area with a stale word before the driver is built and finds none left after; with the clear made a no-op it fails, naming 2690 of 2704 words still stale (the other fourteen are descriptors the rings rewrite).
The crate's 28 tests pass and clippy with warnings denied is clean on it.
Nothing was run on the board.

carry_forward_bullets: Still owed before api-compat-c is complete: a row that witnesses the gossip half of a listener bound late; the gossip multihop key and the multi-hop graph it asks for; a face session's history query destination; the pico ABI's refusal of listen and connect together; a client re-running its search when its first node is lost; a peer starting its responder after its connects as upstream does; the pico ABI sending the Final to an accepted peer.

Not examined: an IPv6 scouting group, which is refused by name; a listener's addresses on a host with no getifaddrs; a router that gossips; a client whose listener binds in the background, which is held and has no row.
Read the hosted CI and Platform runs of this push per job first.
changes_bullets: The runtime gets a bind-phase driver and a background retry loop with eight unit tests; the C ABI reads the listen budget and schedule and binds through the driver.
Endpoints left to the background are bound as tasks of the role and served at once; the scouting responder and the gossip list take the locators of listeners bound late.

One differential row of seven settings, a late-bound Hello shape, four tests on wz alone and four small unit tests are added; the foreign-adjudicator pin moves 1028 to 1029 and the depth pin 242 to 251.
Round 3089.decision_summary: Round 3089 makes a C session retry a bind inside its listen budget and name a listener that bound late. The bind phase tried each endpoint once whatever listen/timeout_ms and listen/retry said, and the carry of Round 3076 named that. MEASURED first on the real library with a port let go 0.7 s in: a non-zero budget retries the bind on the retry schedule; with exit_on_failure true the open is held up until it binds (1004 ms) and fails with -4 at the budget when the port stays taken (604 ms for 600); with it false the open returns at once and the bind goes on in the background; a Scout asked before that bind is answered with no locator and after it with the new one. BUILT: the runtime's bind-phase driver, the C ABI's phase type and reader, a holder for the endpoints left to the background, and a responder that reads the locators of listeners bound after it started. The gossip half is not witnessed. The atom stays partial.
verification_bullets: Measured first on the real library; each differential row asserts the real library's answer before wz's, and the new row and the new Hello shape were green against wz the first time they ran.
Five mutations, each applied alone after the cdylib was rebuilt, each red at the row that names it, and the same tree rebuilt unmutated is green. The gossip half of a late listener has no row.

The whole preflight ran on the committed tree before this entry: clippy on seven targets, the runtime, session-core and ABI suites, Layer C1ch, the rustdoc budget, the cross-impl audit, the C1cn census, the static bundle of 85 gates, the C0 legs after its oracle pin stop and Layer C1cc whole (3793 s), each read from its own exit code. Round 3091.decision_summary: The TC6 interface's software reset had two defects. Its budget counted the delays it had asked for, the shape the first run on a board exposed in a neighbouring driver: a wait promises only at least what it is told, so on a board whose clock ran 44 times slow a 100 ms budget would last minutes. It now takes the clock and ends on elapsed time. And it waited for the device to report a finished reset without first clearing the reset flag a device keeps from power-on, so the old flag could stand for the completion of this reset, which the first chip crate written on the interface showed. It now clears the flag before it resets. Every TC6 device behaves so, which is why the clear belongs in the interface crate and not in a chip crate.

Round 3092.decision_summary: The LAN8650 and LAN8651 became a chip crate over the TC6 interface. Open reads DEVID before anything is written, because OA_PHYID names the PHY and not the product, and refuses a model or revision the documents do not grade; a newer revision is driven only when the config accepts it. It then soft-resets, runs the configuration application note's sequence in its order, sets PLCA, programs the MAC and enables it, and declares sync last. Reset handling is a service call that takes the delay and clock as arguments and reruns the whole bring-up when a footer loses SYNC or a RESETC event arrives, since the data sheet disagrees with itself on whether a PHY-only reset clears SYNC. Its first call also puts collision detection in step with PLCA, which the note's flowchart does not, because a node whose PLCA never comes up would run CSMA/CD with collision detection off.
verification_bullets: The new crate's 43 host tests and the 27 of wz-oa-tc6 pass. Clippy with warnings denied is clean on both crates, tests included, rustfmt and rustdoc with warnings denied are clean, and the crate checks for a bare-metal Arm target.

That the power-on RESETC is cleared before the soft reset is checked here by order; the interface's own test checks that a stale flag cannot complete a reset. No document gives a reset duration, so the harm it prevents is not modelled.

Nothing ran on a chip. The model is a reading of the documents shared with the code, so a misreading would pass both. The configuration registers are described only in the application note, so the data sheet cannot check them.

changes_bullets: A relay holds the chunk each shared-memory slice of a routed Put names, from the Put's arrival until it has been routed, and acknowledges each slice to its sender through the face's handoff; a Push from a face that never negotiated shared memory is counted and not routed, and the reference the message arrived with goes back when the pass ends, on every way out of the routing.

The session core gains the face-side half of upstream's map_to_partner: a relayed send takes a reference for a link whose peer lists the chunk's protocol and sends the descriptor of it, kept once the frame left and given back if it did not, and sends the chunk's bytes in the plain layout, without the marker and with the extension chain renormalised, to any other link.

A received chunk is a buffer a message can be sent from again: the resolver's hold returns a handle whose reservation raises the chunk's count in the provider's header, on top of the reference the descriptor arrived with.
The router's two egress seams, the peer forwarder's one and the router's multicast group send go through the relay; a multicast group negotiates nothing and is always sent the bytes.

carry_forward_bullets: The fields of an extend block are read for syntax only: their numbers, names and types, and whether a number lies in an extension range of the extended message, are not judged although protoc judges them. Two oracle cases and a unit test pin the boundary; closing it needs the extension ranges recorded, which the parser still ignores.

protoc cross-links a message's nested messages before its own fields, and builds every name and number of a file before it resolves any type; the reader links fields first and mixes the two phases. It shows only when one schema holds two errors, and it predates this change.
The refusal of a reached extend or group names the message but not the route by which the root reaches it. A route (pkg.Root -> pkg.Mid -> pkg.Base) would let a consumer show why.
A reached extend is still refused outright. Declaring the message and leaving the extension fields unnamed would be a different contract, and the header does not offer it.

The oracle is now right for the two releases measured (3.21.12 and 3.12.4) and measures the rest of what it can, but a newer protoc has not judged it: its error format, its handling of proto3 optional and editions, and the shape of its descriptor.proto are unchecked, and a root the real-descriptor cases name (for example google.protobuf.DescriptorProto.ExtensionRange) that a future descriptor.proto drops would fail the armed run loudly, as a corpus fault. A newer runner image should run the armed oracle once before its first push.

The door refuses nesting past 31 on every protoc, so a schema nested deeper that protoc 3.12.4 compiles is refused by the door with a reason that says so. That is deliberate and now an explicit category of the oracle; raising the bound would need the bound to follow a protoc, which the door does not know.

protoc --decode has a recursion limit of its own (about 100 levels in 3.12.4), so the oracle's depth probe asks only whether a schema compiles and reads nothing back; a corpus case that nests past that limit and needs the descriptor would fail with the decode message.
The hosted arming still reads descriptor.proto from beside protoc or the Debian and local install paths; a runner that keeps it elsewhere fails the armed run with a message that names the places.

A schema that imports a file declaring an edition is still refused in any file read, the well-known types are still not part of the library, and the command line still has no flag that reads a .proto file.

The header, the module documentation and the discard-site lint state and register the rule; no symbol, document key or revision moved. carry_forward_bullets: The judge is a library type and is not behind a handle. The per-stream state belongs to the capture pipeline, keyed by message, key instance and publisher slot, and fed from the payload seam where the publisher and the record's time are in hand; the declaration of a profile once and its choice per key pattern is the next step and is not built.

The CRC is fed from the length field as received, and the timeout is judged against the previous valid instant on every reception, a CRC error and a repetition included. Both are read from the consumer's written specification; the reference code was not read, so the order of the timeout check and the update on one reception is an inference to confirm there.

The consumer's two vectors are reproduced by an independent model, not by this engine. Running the doors once on a profile built from that document's numbers closes it, with the constants kept out of the repository.

A profile cannot say a rule that depends on a value (a result forced to zero for a query, a sender masked to 28 bits); the caller decides the part values, and a value that does not fit is refused. A CRC field may be wider than the CRC and is then compared whole.

The profile text is read as JSON5 by the workspace reader, so comments and trailing commas are admitted; a strict mode is not offered. A refusal of the profile's content carries a JSON pointer and not a byte offset, so a text box that highlights a place needs the pointer mapped back to the text.
No command-line flag builds or opens a frame, the parity table records that as deliberate, and the body is still produced by the caller: the protobuf encoder from JSON is a later step.

Round 3102.decision_summary: A consumer that produces and analyses payloads behind an end-to-end protection header (a length, an identifier, a CRC, a message cell and a counter, laid out differently per profile, with a CRC fed in a fixed order that is not the wire order) must not carry that arithmetic itself, and this repository is public, so no protocol's constants may live in it. This round built the mechanism and left every constant to the caller: a profile is JSON passed on each call, a generic CRC engine for widths 8 to 64 follows the Rocksoft model, frames are built and opened statelessly, the receiver's counter and timeout rules are a pure library type, and two doors, wz_dissect_e2e_wrap and wz_dissect_e2e_open (ABI 26), answer with a document that shows every step. The CRC is taken over the length field as received, so a differently counted length shows only as information beside a clean CRC. Tests run on synthetic profiles only.

CRC engine (8): the polynomial not reflected, the start value not reflected, the output reflection skipped when only one of refin and refout is set, xorout dropped, the register mask dropped, a polynomial bit off, an unsupported width accepted, a parameter that does not fit accepted. Judge (15): one per rule, including a CRC error moving the baseline or the instant, a repetition moving either, the first reception flagged, the gap off by one, no wrap at the width, a timeout without history, the timeout judged after the move, a backwards clock, a wider counter accepted. Frame (12): the cover fed backwards, the CRC field fed, the length counting fields instead of widths, parts cut before the xor, the xor skipped, a part overflow truncated, the length overflow unchecked, the body extent taken from the length field, a masked CRC comparison, a length verdict always true, a missing or unknown value accepted. Profile validation (18): every refusal shape has a mutant that removes it. Documents (4) and doors (5): a wrong source word, a bare integer, uppercase hex, a null key, the ABI constant, a null body with a length, two non-UTF-8 checks, and the dropped export name, which the Rust tests cannot see and Layer C1bo's link step caught. Without the nesting bound a 200000-level text aborts the test process with a stack overflow. Three things the mutants taught: a mutant (a timeout with no history) was hidden when batched with two others and failed when run alone; the first published CRC sets all have a start value equal to its own reflection, so five sets whose start value is not its own reflection were added and the start-orientation mutant is caught by them first; and a first draft of the length test assumed a different counting rule would fail the CRC, which it cannot, because the CRC is taken over the length field as received.

Five golden frames over five synthetic profiles (CRC first, last and in the middle; 1, 2 and 4 byte counters; 8, 16, 32 and 64 bit CRCs; a CRC field wider than the CRC; 7 and 8 byte fields past 2^53) were computed once by an independent model written from the profile description. Round 3108.decision_summary: The consumer ran the reference receiver and found the judge's timeout rule differing in four places. The owner decided that the judge follows the specification's order: the CRC, then the counter rules and the state update, then the timeout against the instant as it then stands. A valid frame therefore clears its own timeout however long the silence before it was, while a CRC error and a repetition move nothing and are judged against the previous valid instant. An information field, silence_ms, reports the silence before each reception or poll without changing a boolean; it is measured from the same instant the timeout uses, so a timeout is never reported beside nothing. arm() starts the silence clock of a stream that never received, without creating history. A backwards clock still counts as no time passed, deliberately unlike a fixed-width device clock. The earlier inference that the timeout is judged before the update was wrong.

carry_forward_bullets: The session fold hands a lowlatency unit to the reader whole, as one message, and both doors decline a unit that holds a message followed by more bytes. Upstream's sender writes one message per unit, but its receiver loops over a unit (the lowlatency rx read_messages), so a peer that packed several would read fully upstream and be declined here. Splitting a lean unit is the fold's decision to take, and the door follows it.

The door cannot know a message's position in its session, so a first byte in neither MID space, and the transport MIDs a lean link does not carry after its handshake (Frame, Fragment, Join, transport Oam), read as the context-free door reads them where the document declines the row. A test derives that set over all 256 header bytes against the fold's rule; making the door refuse them would need the direction and whether its Open has passed, which the context object does not carry.

A malformed context is WZ_DISSECT_ERR_INVALID_ARG with no string, on the rule that code writes a context. If a consumer builds contexts by hand and wants to be told which key is wrong, the alternative is its own error code and a diagnose door in the selector's shape; the Rust reader already names the key (ContextRefusal).

Only lowlatency changes how a message reads today. If another capability ever does, it enters MessageContext and the context reader together, and the header's list of keys the door ignores changes with it; the round-trip test against the document's writer is what would show a key renamed under it.

The consumer's own captures were not run through the new door: the sessions in the tests are built from this repository's codecs and the protocol layout. A run of the real lowlatency capture through the built library is the check that remains.

The context reader and the door depend on the fold's tri-state cells: the document writes `lowlatency` as null until the Init pair is seen, and the reader treats `negotiated: false` as unknown on top of that. If the writer's null rule ever moves, the round trip over 258 real sessions is what shows it; the extra `negotiated` filter in the reader is then the only guard for a hand-built context that says `true` beside `negotiated: false`.

Round 3109.decision_summary: A consumer reading a LowLatency session one message at a time got every data message back as Unknown, with only header, mid, z and body, while the session's field document named and decoded the same bytes in full. The cause was that the one-message door has no session: its transport walker has no arm for a network MID, whereas the document reads a lean unit through the network walker, which the fold picks per direction once that direction has sent its Open. A new door, wz_dissect_transport_message_in, takes the flow's context object and reads a message with the same walker the document's row uses. With LowLatency agreed, a first byte in the network MID space reads as the network message and any other as a transport message; an unagreed or unknown capability reads as the old door does. The old door and every document are unchanged. The ABI revision moves to 27; no document revision moves, since the answer is a field tree.

changes_bullets: The session core gains the sending half of the handoff as a trait an authenticator may operate. An Open message names the counters the authenticator leased and names the block disabled, as before, when it operates none. A message that carries a buffer of shared memory, which is the payload of a Put, the value of a query or the payload of a reply, is sent inside a transaction that counts each slice and keeps its chunk, committed when the message left and given back when it did not.

The runtime's auth segment leases a band of counters per session, zeroed whatever the last holder left, from a pool that serves 351 sessions of eight bands and then declares the block disabled. Each slice adds one to its band's counter and keeps the chunk confirmed by the watchdog bit alone, without touching the reference count, and the watchdog thread's tick lets go of as many of the oldest chunks of a band as the peer has lowered the counter by. Declaring the counters again forgets what the last peer was owed.

Two late reader legs in the payload interop file: wz sends to a subscriber of upstream that reads a second late and the sample must arrive as shared memory, and the number of chunks wz keeps confirmed must be back to what it was before the send; upstream's own sender to the same subscriber is the control. Round 3110.decision_summary: Round 3110 closes the clause of transport-shm that Round 3104 named first among those left: the counters wz declares as a sender. It was measured before it was built, and it was a real defect. A buffer's owner lets go of it the moment it is sent, the chunk's watchdog bit is confirmed only while somebody holds it, and upstream's validator invalidates an unconfirmed chunk within 100 ms, so wz sending to upstream's own subscriber that read a second late delivered nothing while upstream's own publisher sending to the same subscriber delivered. Upstream's sender keeps a hard reference to every buffer it sends until the receiver lowers a counter the sender named in its Open message, and wz named none and kept none. It now leases counters per session, declares them in both Open messages, counts every slice it sends and keeps its chunk confirmed until the peer has acknowledged it. The atom stays partial and REMAINING WORK does not move.

A new type for the end, with the two words and a walk over them, sits beside the link kind and the address family. A handshake records no end, a duplicate row is dropped, and the receiving end is never recorded.

The census document gains an always present array, ends, in the node plane beside links, each row holding node (an index into the nodes), sender_end (low or high) and flow. Revision 20 declares the keys ends, node and sender_end, the sender_end family as a passenger and the key set; the key is not end because revision 19 writes end as a number in the ambiguity report.
